web_title: 3. Unit Economics, Margins & Cash Conversion Forensics
book_title: Chapter 3: The Profit-to-Cash Chasm — Where the ₹527 Crore EBITDA Goes
question: Why does a business earning 25% EBITDA margins and 21.3% ROCE generate negative cumulative Free Cash Flow of -₹847 crore over three years?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an accounting opinion; inventory sitting on a shop floor for 453 days is a physical reality that your bank balance has to finance.
epigraph.author: Forensic Capital Goods Rule

web_blocks.html: On the income statement, Jyoti CNC Automation looks like a textbook margin-expansion story. Between FY23 and FY26, consolidated sales more than doubled from ₹929 crore to ₹2,093 crore [1]. Operating profit (EBITDA) jumped nearly seven-fold from ₹77 crore (8% OPM) to ₹527 crore (25% OPM) [1]. Per the FY26 Annual Report, material costs fell 286 basis points from 50.86% of sales in FY25 to 48.00% in FY26 [2]. That mix shift toward 5-axis and custom machines lifted gross margin to 55.1% [2]. Employee costs rose from ₹258.22 crore (14.2% of sales) in FY25 to ₹330.02 crore (15.8% of sales) in FY26 [13]. Management added staff ahead of the 16,000-machine capacity ramp [13]. Look at FY26 through a per-₹100 sales lens [1]. Operating expenses take ₹74.82, leaving ₹25.18 in EBITDA [1]. After ₹2.39 for depreciation, ₹3.34 for interest, and ₹2.87 in other income (₹60 Cr in FY26 vs. ₹5 Cr in FY25), pre-tax profit is ₹22.31 [1]. Net profit is ₹16.05 per ₹100 of sales [1]. Yet only ₹2.58 reaches Cash Flow from Operations (CFO), while -₹14.43 exits for investing activities [1].

web_blocks.caption: FY26 Consolidated P&L to Free Cash Flow Waterfall (₹ Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Of ₹527 Cr in FY26 EBITDA (25.2% margin) and ₹336 Cr in Net Profit, only ₹54 Cr reached Operating Cash Flow (34% pre-tax CFO/EBITDA) because working capital absorbed cash; after ₹323 Cr capex, Free Cash Flow was -₹269 Cr.

web_blocks.html: The main forensic tension at Jyoti CNC sits below the EBITDA line. Across the FY24–FY26 boom, Jyoti posted cumulative Net Profit of ₹803 crore (₹151 Cr + ₹316 Cr + ₹336 Cr) [1]. Over those same three years, cumulative Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) was -₹99 crore (-₹48 Cr in FY24, -₹105 Cr in FY25, and +₹54 Cr in FY26) [1]. Cumulative Free Cash Flow (FCF) was -₹847 crore (-₹163 Cr, -₹415 Cr, and -₹269 Cr) [1]. Pre-tax CFO-to-EBITDA conversion stood at 1% in FY24, -4% in FY25, and 34% in FY26 [1]. That sits well below the >70% mark of disciplined industrial compounders [1]. On the balance sheet, Other Assets (mainly inventory and receivables) surged by ₹1,775 crore from March 2023 (₹1,214 Cr) to September 2026 (₹2,989 Cr) [1]. Meanwhile, Other Liabilities rose by just ₹298 crore, from ₹598 Cr to ₹896 Cr [1]. That gap required ₹937 crore of net financing inflows across FY24–FY26 to fund working capital and capex [1].

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital, Cash Conversion & Re-Leveraging Trajectory (FY23–Sep 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Inventory days jumped 75 days in FY26 to 453 days and debtor days climbed to 104 days, pushing Working Capital Days from -48 (FY23) to 234 (FY26) and forcing borrowings back up to ₹946 Cr.

web_blocks.html: Why is so much cash trapped on the balance sheet? Four structural drivers explain the gap. First, custom aerospace and defence 5-axis machines take 3 to 18 months to build [7]. Jyoti also stocked up on imported CNC controllers as global lead times doubled [6]. Together, those factors pushed Inventory Days from 378 in FY25 to 453 days in FY26, while CRISIL noted gross current assets near ~443 days [1][6][7]. Second, Debtor Days nearly doubled from 57 days in FY23 to 104 days in FY26 as large industrial and defence buyers took longer to pay [1]. Third, Days Payable fell from 273 days in FY23 to 198 days in FY26 as Jyoti paid suppliers faster after the IPO [1]. That stretched the Cash Conversion Cycle to 359 days [1]. Working Capital Days flipped from -48 days (when client advances funded operations) to +234 days [1]. Fourth, Huron shifted to dispatch-based revenue recognition under French export-control scrutiny [6]. That left ~₹60 crore of H1 FY27 dispatches unbooked in sales even though costs were already paid [6]. As a result, debt tripled from ₹304 crore (Mar 2024) to ₹946 crore (Sep 2026) [1]. Quarterly interest costs climbed back from ₹9 crore in Sep 2024 to ₹20–24 crore across Dec 2025–Jun 2026, reaching ₹82 Cr TTM [1].

Two other P&L items below the operating line also merit tracking. First, depreciation rose from ₹33 crore (FY24) and ₹36 crore (FY25) to ₹50 crore in FY26 and ₹59 crore TTM [1]. Quarterly depreciation doubled from ₹8 crore in Sep 2023 to ₹16 crore in Sep 2026 as new Rajkot bays came online [1]. Second, the effective tax rate normalized after wild turnaround swings (175% in FY23 on ₹7 Cr PBT, 18% in FY24) to 24% in FY25 and 28% in FY26 [1]. Quarterly Other Income also swung between -₹0 crore (Dec 2024–Mar 2025) and ₹25 crore (Mar 2026) [1].

web_blocks.mechanism: Okuma is a top Japanese CNC builder with deep mechatronic vertical integration. It builds its own OSP CNC controllers, servos, and spindles while managing global industrial capex cycles.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: It keeps a net-cash or low-debt balance sheet and positive through-cycle FCF conversion. That discipline lets it absorb 20–30% cyclical order drops without equity dilution or distress.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: True compounder status in CNC tools requires owning controller electronics AND turning peak EBITDA into cash, not debt-funded inventory. Until CFO/EBITDA tops 65–70% and debt falls, Jyoti remains a cyclical capital-goods play.

book_paragraphs: Now we arrive at the single most important forensic puzzle in the entire Jyoti CNC story. Pull up the profit-and-loss statement for FY26 and it looks like a dream: ₹2,093 crore of revenue, a 55.1% gross margin—meaning raw materials consumed just 48.00% of sales, down 286 basis points from 50.86% in FY25—₹527 crore of operating profit at a 25% margin, and ₹336 crore of net profit. In fact, over the last three fiscal years from FY24 to FY26, Jyoti reported ₹803 crore in cumulative net profit.

Let's translate FY26 into simple ₹100 unit economics so you can see where every rupee goes. Out of every ₹100 of sales, ₹74.82 pays for raw castings, imported controllers, employee salaries—which rose from ₹258.22 crore (14.2% of sales) in FY25 to ₹330.02 crore (15.8% of sales) in FY26 as Rajkot hired ahead of its 16,000-machine expansion—and factory overheads. That leaves ₹25.18 of operating EBITDA. Subtract ₹2.39 for depreciation, ₹3.34 for interest, add ₹2.87 of other income (which jumped to ₹60 crore in FY26 from ₹5 crore in FY25), and pay taxes, and you are left with ₹16.05 of net profit per ₹100 of revenue.

Now flip the page to the cash flow statement, and watch what happens when you and I follow the actual cash. Out of that ₹16.05 of net profit per ₹100 of revenue, only ₹2.58 actually showed up as Cash Flow from Operations! Meanwhile, ₹14.43 walked straight back out the door for capital expenditure and investing activities. Across all three boom years from FY24 through FY26, cumulative Cash Flow from Operations was negative ₹99 crore—minus ₹48 crore in FY24, minus ₹105 crore in FY25, and barely positive ₹54 crore in FY26. Add in capex, and Jyoti CNC burned negative ₹847 crore in Free Cash Flow across three straight years of record profitability, relying on ₹937 crore of net financing inflows to bridge the gap.

How can a business earn ₹336 crore on paper in FY26 and yet end the year ₹269 crore deeper in Free Cash Flow deficit? Look at the balance sheet and working capital ratios, and the mystery vanishes. Between March 2023 and September 2026, Other Assets—mostly inventory and receivables—swelled from ₹1,214 crore to ₹2,989 crore, an expansion of ₹1,775 crore! Over that same span, Other Liabilities rose by only ₹298 crore, from ₹598 crore to ₹896 crore. That means Jyoti had to finance almost ₹1,477 crore of net working-asset growth out of its own pocket and borrowings.

Break that down into days, and you can feel the weight on the shop floor. In FY26, Inventory Days jumped 75 days in a single year, from 378 days to 453 days—more than fifteen months of cost of goods sitting as raw castings, imported Fanuc and Siemens controllers, and half-built 5-axis machines. At the same time, Debtor Days crept steadily higher, from 57 days in FY23 to 68 in FY24, 98 in FY25, and 104 days in FY26, as large industrial and defence buyers took longer to settle invoices.

Meanwhile, Days Payable dropped from 273 days in FY23 to 198 days in FY26 because a flush post-IPO Jyoti paid its vendors faster. Put those three numbers together—453 days of inventory plus 104 days of receivables minus 198 days of payables—and Jyoti's Cash Conversion Cycle stretches to 359 days, practically an entire calendar year between paying for steel and controllers and collecting cash from the customer. Even more telling, Working Capital Days flipped from minus 48 days in FY23—when customer advances financed the shop floor—to plus 234 days in FY26. That 282-day swing didn't just eat all of Jyoti's ₹803 crore of accounting profit; it ate the ₹360 crore of IPO working-capital cash and forced management to borrow all over again.

Look at the borrowings line on the balance sheet—it tells the story with brutal clarity. In March 2023, before the IPO, debt stood at ₹835 crore. The January 2024 IPO paid it down to ₹304 crore. Two and a half years later, in September 2026, borrowings are back up to ₹946 crore—₹111 crore higher than before the IPO! And quarterly interest expense has climbed back from ₹9 crore in September 2024 to ₹20–24 crore in recent quarters, or ₹82 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis. At the same time, quarterly depreciation has doubled from ₹8 crore in September 2023 to ₹16 crore in September 2026 (₹59 crore trailing twelve-month) as newly commissioned Rajkot capacity enters the books, and effective tax rates have normalized to 24–28% after wild turnaround swings.

Management has a fair operational explanation for part of this: global CNC controller lead times doubled, so Jyoti deliberately stocked up on critical electronics to ship 1,911 machines in Q2 FY27, while aerospace machines naturally sit in work-in-progress for three to eighteen months and ₹60 crore of Huron's H1 FY27 dispatches sat unbooked awaiting export clearances. Compare that with Japan's Okuma Corporation, which builds its own OSP controllers and protects a fortress net-cash balance sheet precisely because machine tools are brutally cyclical. Until Jyoti turns 453-day inventory into 65%-plus CFO-to-EBITDA cash conversion, every rupee of growth requires fresh debt.

Let's put this into practical capital-allocation terms so you never lose sight of the core risk. In FY24, pre-tax CFO-to-EBITDA conversion was just 1%. In FY25, it was minus 4%. In FY26, it improved to 34%—still barely half of the 65%-to-70% threshold you want to see in a self-funding industrial franchise. When a company grows revenue from ₹929 crore to ₹2,286 crore trailing twelve-month while converting only a third of EBITDA into operating cash, growth itself becomes a cash consumer rather than a cash generator. Every incremental ₹100 crore of aerospace or EMS revenue currently demands extra working capital upfront before the final invoice clears.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The waterfall in FY26 is an x-ray of capital-intensive growth: ₹100 of revenue yields ₹25.18 of EBITDA and ₹16.05 of Net Profit, yet only ₹2.58 reaches Operating Cash Flow before ₹14.43 goes out the door for investing capex. You and I must never confuse a 25% EBITDA margin with a self-funding compounder.

book_callouts.title: THE WORKING-CAPITAL FLIP
book_callouts.text: In FY23, Working Capital Days were minus 48—suppliers and customer advances funded the business. By FY26, Working Capital Days hit plus 234. That 282-day swing is the exact reason ₹803 crore of three-year net profit produced minus ₹847 crore of Free Cash Flow.

book_callouts.title: WATCH OTHER INCOME LUMPINESS
book_callouts.text: Notice that FY26 Other Income jumped to ₹60 crore (including ₹20 crore in June 2025 and ₹25 crore in March 2026) from just ₹5 crore in FY25. When evaluating core machine-tool profitability, always strip out non-operating other income and track standalone EBITDA and CFO.
